learn.hook: Have you ever searched the whole house for something that was right in front of you? Let's read a funny story about that!
points: A humorous story is a funny story that makes us smile or laugh.
The fun often comes from a surprise, a silly mistake or a mix-up.
Family stories show how family members care for, help and laugh with each other.
While reading, ask: Who is in the story? What happened? Why is it funny?
To answer a question, go back and find the line that gives the answer.

example.q: Read: Dadi could not find her glasses. She looked under the sofa and behind the TV. She even looked in Bholu the cat's basket. 'Who has hidden my glasses?' she cried. Little Tara giggled and pointed at the fruit bowl. There they were, resting on a mango! Dadi had put them down while choosing fruit. The whole family laughed, and Dadi laughed the loudest. Why did the family laugh?
steps: Find where the glasses were: on a mango in the fruit bowl.
Find who put them there: Dadi herself, while choosing fruit.
Think: Dadi blamed someone else, but it was her own mix-up. That surprise is funny.
example.answer: They laughed because Dadi thought someone had hidden her glasses, but she had left them on a mango herself.

learn.reallife: In our families, someone is always looking for keys, a phone or the TV remote. These little mix-ups become the funny stories we tell again and again.

games.title: Story in order
games.prompt: Put the story events in the order they happened
items: She searches under the sofa and behind the TV.
She asks who has hidden her glasses.
Tara points at the fruit bowl.

games.title: Story words
pairs: laughed in a light, silly way

quiz.q: Read: 'Dadi could not find her glasses. She looked under the sofa and behind the TV. She even looked in Bholu the cat's basket.' Which place did Dadi NOT search?
quiz.explain: The passage names the sofa, the TV and the cat's basket. It never says she looked inside the cupboard.
quiz.mistake: Picks a place without checking the lines of the passage

quiz.q: Read: ''Who has hidden my glasses?' Dadi cried.' What did Dadi think had happened?
options: The cat had eaten her glasses
She had given her glasses away
quiz.explain: Her question 'Who has hidden my glasses?' shows she thought someone had hidden them.
quiz.mistake: Guesses instead of reading Dadi's exact words

quiz.q: Read: 'Little Tara giggled and pointed at the fruit bowl. There they were, resting on a mango!' Where were the glasses?
options: On a mango in the fruit bowl
quiz.explain: The lines say the glasses were resting on a mango in the fruit bowl.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the places Dadi searched with the place the glasses were found

quiz.q: Read: 'Dadi had put them down while choosing fruit.' Who had put the glasses on the mango?
quiz.explain: The line clearly says Dadi had put them down while choosing fruit.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the child who found the glasses must have hidden them

quiz.q: What makes Dadi's story funny?
options: She blamed others, but she had left the glasses there herself
Tara hid the glasses as a trick
quiz.explain: The surprise is that the 'missing' glasses were left by Dadi herself. A mix-up like this is what makes the story humorous.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that a surprising mix-up is the source of humour

quiz.q: Read: 'Little Tara giggled.' What does 'giggled' mean?
options: Laughed in a light, silly way
quiz.explain: To giggle is to laugh lightly, often in a silly or nervous way.
quiz.mistake: Confuses giggle with other sounds people make

quiz.q: Read: 'The whole family laughed, and Dadi laughed the loudest.' What does this tell us about Dadi?
options: She could laugh at her own mistake
quiz.explain: Laughing the loudest shows Dadi enjoyed the joke, even though the mistake was her own.
quiz.mistake: Expects a person who made a mistake to feel only upset

quiz.q: Which of these is most likely to be part of a humorous story?
options: A funny mix-up that makes readers laugh
quiz.explain: Humorous stories are written to amuse us, often through mix-ups and surprises.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what 'humorous' means

teach.ask: Gappu flaps in: 'Tweet! What makes a story humorous? And how do I find answers in a passage?'
teach.praise: Ha ha! Now I know funny stories have mix-ups and surprises, and the answers hide in the lines!
teach.nudge: But what makes the story funny? And where do I look for the answer?

learn.hook: Your Papa has a brother and your Mummy has a sister. What do you call them in English? Let's learn family words!
points: Family words name our relations: father, mother, brother, sister, grandfather, grandmother.
Your father's or mother's brother is your uncle. Their sister is your aunt.
The children of your uncle or aunt are your cousins.
Your brother's or sister's son is your nephew. Their daughter is your niece.
Masculine words name males (uncle, king). Feminine words name females (aunt, queen). Some words like cousin, friend and child can be used for both.

example.q: Riya's mother's brother is visiting for Raksha Bandhan. Riya calls him Mama ji. What is the English family word for him?
steps: He is the brother of Riya's mother.
A parent's brother is called an uncle in English.
example.answer: Uncle

learn.reallife: At weddings and festivals, we meet many relatives. Knowing family words helps us introduce them: 'This is my aunt, and this is my cousin Aarav.'

quiz.q: What is the feminine of 'nephew'?
quiz.explain: A nephew is a brother's or sister's son. A daughter in the same place is a niece.
quiz.mistake: Makes a feminine by adding '-ess' to every word

quiz.q: What is the masculine of 'aunt'?
quiz.explain: Aunt and uncle are a pair: aunt is feminine, uncle is masculine.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the pairs of family words

quiz.q: Your father's father is your ___.
quiz.explain: The father of your parent is your grandfather.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a parent's father with a parent's brother

quiz.q: Your aunt's daughter is your ___.
quiz.explain: The children of your aunts and uncles are your cousins.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any girl relative younger than a parent is a niece

quiz.q: Which word can be used for both a boy and a girl?
quiz.explain: A cousin can be a boy or a girl. Brother and king are masculine; niece is feminine.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that some nouns are common to both genders

quiz.q: What is the feminine of 'king'?
quiz.explain: King and queen are a masculine-feminine pair. Princess is the feminine of prince.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up king-queen with prince-princess

quiz.q: Meera's brother has a son. What is the son to Meera?
quiz.explain: A brother's or sister's son is your nephew.
quiz.mistake: Confuses nephew with cousin

quiz.q: What is the masculine of 'lioness'?
quiz.explain: We add '-ess' to lion to make lioness. So the masculine is lion.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that '-ess' was added to make the feminine

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Who is my uncle, who is my cousin, and what are masculine and feminine words?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Now I can name my whole bird family in English!
teach.nudge: Who is my uncle? And what is the difference between masculine and feminine words?

learn.hook: 'Where are my spectacles?' 'Oh no, I sat on them!' Each of these sentences needs a different mark at the end. Can you spot them?
points: A telling sentence (statement) ends with a full stop (.): Papa is reading the newspaper.
An asking sentence (question) ends with a question mark (?): Where are my spectacles?
A sentence that shows strong feeling ends with an exclamation mark (!): What a funny face!
An order or a request usually ends with a full stop: Please pass the chutney.
Every sentence begins with a capital letter. Names of people and places begin with capitals too.

example.q: Write it correctly: where did chacha keep his spectacles
steps: It begins a sentence, so 'where' becomes 'Where'.
'Chacha' is a name, so it gets a capital C.
It asks something, so it ends with a question mark.
example.answer: Where did Chacha keep his spectacles?

learn.reallife: Messages to family, notes on the fridge and school homework all need the right capital letters and end marks so the reader understands you.

quiz.q: Which mark should end this sentence: 'Where is my tiffin box'
quiz.explain: The sentence asks something, so it ends with a question mark.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice that 'Where' starts a question

quiz.q: Which sentence shows strong feeling?
quiz.explain: 'What a funny joke!' shows surprise and joy, and it ends with an exclamation mark.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence about something funny is an exclamation

quiz.q: In 'my cousin lives in jaipur.', which words need capital letters?
quiz.explain: 'My' is the first word of the sentence, and 'Jaipur' is the name of a place. Both need capitals: My cousin lives in Jaipur.
quiz.mistake: Forgets capitals for names of places or for the first word

quiz.q: What kind of sentence is 'Please close the door.'?
quiz.explain: It asks someone politely to do something, so it is a request. It ends with a full stop.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every polite sentence must be a question

quiz.q: Papa cannot read without his spectacles. What are spectacles?
quiz.explain: Spectacles is another word for glasses that help people see clearly.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the word 'spectacles'

quiz.q: Choose the right word: 'Papa wears a pair of ___.'
quiz.explain: We say 'a pair of spectacles', just like 'a pair of scissors'. The word is used in the plural.
quiz.mistake: Uses the singular after 'a pair of'

quiz.q: A full stop at the end of a sentence usually shows that the sentence ___.
quiz.explain: Telling sentences, and also orders and requests, end with a full stop.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the jobs of the different end marks

quiz.q: Which of these needs a question mark?
options: Please keep a laddoo for me
quiz.explain: 'Who ate the last laddoo' asks something, so it needs a question mark.
quiz.mistake: Picks a sentence just because it mentions the laddoo

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his feathers: 'When do I use a full stop, a question mark and an exclamation mark?'
teach.praise: Wow! Now my sentences will always end the right way!
teach.nudge: Which mark goes after a question? And which one shows strong feeling?

learn.hook: Vroom, vroom... cough, cough... STOP! What happens when a scooter trip does not go as planned? Let's find out!
points: An adventure is an exciting trip or happening, often with a problem to solve.
Adventure stories keep us wondering: What will happen next?
The characters face a problem and find a way to solve it.
Look for clues about how the characters feel: scared, tired, excited, happy.
Safety matters on every ride: riders wear helmets and follow traffic rules.

example.q: Read: Last Sunday, Chachu took me to the lake on his old red scooter. We both wore our helmets. On the way, the scooter began to cough and splutter. Then it stopped near a sugarcane field! We pushed it along the road for a long time. A kind farmer gave us water and showed us a repair shop. By evening we reached the lake, tired, dusty and very happy. What problem did Chachu and the narrator face, and how was it solved?
steps: Find the problem: the scooter coughed, spluttered and stopped near a sugarcane field.
Find the help: a kind farmer gave water and showed them a repair shop.
Put it together: problem, then help, then a happy ending at the lake.
example.answer: The scooter broke down; they pushed it, and a kind farmer showed them a repair shop, so they reached the lake by evening.

learn.reallife: Family trips on bikes, buses or trains often have small surprises, like a flat tyre or a late train. Telling them later makes a great adventure story!

games.title: True or false? (from the story)
items: Chachu and the narrator wore helmets.
The story says, 'We both wore our helmets.'
The scooter stopped near a mango orchard.
It stopped near a sugarcane field.
He gave them water and showed them a repair shop.
They reached the lake in the morning.
They reached the lake by evening.
At the end, they were tired but happy.
They were 'tired, dusty and very happy'.

games.title: What happened first?
games.prompt: Put the events of the trip in order
items: Chachu and the narrator set off on the scooter.
The scooter began to cough and splutter.
The scooter stopped near a sugarcane field.
A farmer showed them a repair shop.
They reached the lake by evening.

quiz.q: Read: 'Last Sunday, Chachu took me to the lake on his old red scooter.' Who took the narrator to the lake?
quiz.explain: The line says Chachu took the narrator to the lake.
quiz.mistake: Picks another person from the story without checking the line

quiz.q: Read: 'Then it stopped near a sugarcane field!' Where did the scooter stop?
quiz.explain: The line says it stopped near a sugarcane field.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up where the trip ended with where the scooter stopped

quiz.q: Read: 'A kind farmer gave us water and showed us a repair shop.' How did the farmer help?
options: He drove them to the lake
He gave water and showed them a repair shop
quiz.explain: The farmer gave water and showed them where the repair shop was.
quiz.mistake: Adds details that are not in the passage

quiz.q: Read: 'The scooter began to cough and splutter.' What does this tell us?
options: Something was going wrong with the scooter
quiz.explain: A scooter cannot really cough. These sound words show the engine was having trouble.
quiz.mistake: Takes the words 'cough and splutter' literally

quiz.q: Read: 'By evening we reached the lake, tired, dusty and very happy.' How did they feel at the end?
quiz.explain: The line says they were tired, dusty and very happy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a hard trip must end with sad feelings

quiz.q: Read: 'We both wore our helmets.' Why do riders wear helmets?
quiz.explain: A helmet protects the head if the rider falls. It is a safety rule for everyone on a two-wheeler.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect helmets with safety

quiz.q: Read: 'A kind farmer gave us water.' Which word describes the farmer?
quiz.explain: 'Kind' tells us what the farmer was like. It is a describing word.
quiz.mistake: Picks the action word instead of the describing word

quiz.q: Which of these makes a story an adventure?
options: A list of things to buy
An exciting journey with a problem to solve
quiz.explain: Adventure stories have exciting events and problems that the characters must solve.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what an adventure story is

teach.ask: Gappu bounces: 'What makes a story an adventure? Tell me about the scooter trip!'
teach.praise: Vroom! That was a super adventure. I love how they solved the problem!
teach.nudge: What went wrong on the trip? And how did they solve it?

topics.title: Telling a story in the past

learn.hook: Stories about yesterday need special verbs. 'Today I go' becomes 'Yesterday I went'. Let's learn the past tense!
points: We tell about things that already happened using the simple past tense.
Many verbs just add -ed: push becomes pushed, walk becomes walked.
Some change their spelling: stop becomes stopped, carry becomes carried.
Some verbs change completely: go-went, take-took, ride-rode, see-saw, give-gave, buy-bought.
With 'did' we use the base verb: Did you go? We did not go.

example.q: Change to the past: 'We ride to the market and buy mangoes.'
steps: Find the verbs: ride and buy.
'Ride' changes to 'rode'.
'Buy' changes to 'bought'.
example.answer: We rode to the market and bought mangoes.

learn.reallife: When you tell your friends about your holiday or write a diary, you use the past tense: 'I visited Nani. We ate mangoes.'

quiz.q: What is the past tense of 'go'?
quiz.explain: 'Go' is an irregular verb. Its simple past is 'went'.
quiz.mistake: Adds -ed to every verb

quiz.q: What is the past tense of 'stop'?
quiz.explain: For short words like 'stop', we double the last letter before adding -ed: stopped.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the last consonant

quiz.q: What is the past tense of 'carry'?
quiz.explain: When a word ends in a consonant + y, change y to i and add -ed: carried.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the 'y' when adding -ed

quiz.q: Choose the right word: 'Yesterday, the mechanic ___ Chachu's scooter.'
quiz.explain: 'Yesterday' tells us it happened in the past, so we use 'fixed'.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the time word 'yesterday'

quiz.q: Choose the right word: 'Did you ___ the lake?'
quiz.explain: After 'did', we use the base form of the verb: see.
quiz.mistake: Uses the past form after 'did'

quiz.q: What is the past tense of 'buy'?
quiz.explain: Buy changes to 'bought'. 'Brought' is the past of 'bring', a different verb.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'bought' with 'brought'

quiz.q: What is the past tense of 'catch'?
quiz.explain: 'Catch' is irregular. Its past is 'caught'.
quiz.mistake: Adds -ed to an irregular verb

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the past tense?
options: We push the scooter to the shop.
We pushed the scooter to the shop.
We will push the scooter to the shop.
We are pushing the scooter to the shop.
quiz.explain: 'Pushed' ends in -ed and shows the action is over.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up present, future and past forms

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I change a verb to talk about yesterday?'
teach.praise: Yesterday I learnt the past tense! See? I used it already!
teach.nudge: What do we add to most verbs for the past? And what about verbs like 'go'?

learn.hook: Every story has a storyteller. Sometimes the storyteller is in the story, and sometimes not. Can you tell which?
points: The narrator is the person who tells the story.
In first-person narration, the narrator is part of the story and says I, me, my, we and us.
In third-person narration, the narrator tells about others using he, she, they, his and her.
Sequence words like first, then, next, after that and finally tell the order of events.
A good story has a beginning, a middle and an end.

example.q: Read: 'I held on tight as the scooter went down the hill.' Is this first-person or third-person narration?
steps: Look at who is speaking: the word 'I' is used.
'I' means the narrator is part of the story.
example.answer: First-person narration

learn.reallife: When you tell your class 'I went to the zoo', you are a first-person narrator. A news reporter telling about a match is a third-person narrator.

games.title: Sequence words
games.prompt: Put the steps of getting ready for the ride in order
items: Next, we put on our helmets.
Finally, we rode off down the road.

quiz.q: Read: 'I held on tight as the scooter went down the hill.' Who is telling this?
options: Someone who is not in the story
A narrator who is in the story
quiz.explain: The word 'I' shows the narrator is part of the story. This is first-person narration.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the word 'I'

quiz.q: Which sentence is written in the third person?
options: I parked the scooter near the gate.
We parked the scooter near the gate.
She parked the scooter near the gate.
My brother and I parked the scooter.
quiz.explain: 'She' tells about someone else, so it is third person.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'we' is third person

quiz.q: Which sequence word shows the last event?
quiz.explain: 'Finally' tells us this is the last thing that happened.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up words for the start and the end

quiz.q: Choose the missing word: 'First, we wore helmets. ___, Chachu started the scooter. Finally, we rode away.'
quiz.explain: The middle step needs a word like 'then'. 'Finally' and 'In the end' are for the last step.
quiz.mistake: Uses an ending word for a middle step

quiz.q: The person who tells a story is called the ___.
quiz.explain: The narrator tells the story. It can be a character or someone outside the story.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the main character always tells the story

quiz.q: Which word shows first-person narration?
quiz.explain: 'We' includes the narrator, so it shows first-person narration.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up first-person and third-person pronouns

quiz.q: Rohan wrote: 'Rohan and his father went to Ooty.' How would he say it in the first person?
options: My father and I went to Ooty.
Rohan and his father went to Ooty.
He and his father went to Ooty.
They went to Ooty without him.
quiz.explain: In the first person, Rohan talks about himself as 'I' and 'my'.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the name or 'he' instead of using 'I'

quiz.q: What is the right order for the parts of a story?
quiz.explain: A story starts with a beginning, moves through the middle and finishes with an end.
quiz.mistake: Does not know how stories are built

teach.ask: Gappu peeps: 'Who is a narrator? How do I know if a story is first person or third person?'
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! I am the narrator of my own nest story now!
teach.nudge: Who tells the story? Which words show first person and which show third person?

learn.hook: A rainbow is like a surprise gift after the rain. Poets love to write about it. Let's read a little rainbow poem!
points: A poem is written in lines. A group of lines is called a stanza.
Rhyming words end with the same sound: new-hue, bright-light, rain-train.
Poets use word pictures (imagery) so we can see, hear and feel what they describe.
Reading a poem aloud helps us enjoy its rhythm, like the beat of a song.
A poet may call one thing by another name, like calling a rainbow 'a painted bridge'.

example.q: Read the poem: After the rain, the sky is new, / A shining bow of every hue. / Red and orange, yellow bright, / Green and blue in golden light, / Indigo and violet too, / A painted bridge for me and you! Which words rhyme with 'too'?
steps: Look at the line that ends with 'too': 'Indigo and violet too'.
Look at the next line's last word: 'you'.
'Too' and 'you' end with the same sound.
example.answer: 'You' rhymes with 'too' (and 'new' and 'hue' have the same sound too).

learn.reallife: Songs, nursery rhymes and film songs all use rhyming words. That is why they are so easy to remember!

games.title: About the poem
items: In the poem, the rainbow comes after the rain.
The first line says, 'After the rain, the sky is new'.
The poem calls the rainbow 'a painted bridge'.
The last line calls it 'A painted bridge for me and you!'
The poem says the rainbow comes out at night.
The poem talks about golden light after the rain, not night.

quiz.q: Read: 'Red and orange, yellow bright, / Green and blue in golden light.' Which word rhymes with 'bright'?
quiz.explain: 'Bright' and 'light' both end with the same '-ight' sound.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that is in the poem but does not sound the same at the end

quiz.q: Read: 'After the rain, the sky is new.' When does the rainbow appear in the poem?
quiz.explain: The first line says 'After the rain'.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the first line carefully

quiz.q: Read: 'A shining bow of every hue.' Why does the poet call the rainbow a 'bow'?
options: Because it is curved like a bow
Because it is straight like a stick
quiz.explain: An archer's bow is curved. The rainbow has the same curved shape.
quiz.mistake: Does not picture the shape the poet is comparing

quiz.q: Read: 'A shining bow of every hue.' What does 'hue' mean?
quiz.explain: Hue is another word for colour. 'Every hue' means every colour.
quiz.mistake: Guesses the meaning without using clues from the poem

quiz.q: Read: 'Red and orange, yellow bright, / Green and blue in golden light, / Indigo and violet too.' How many rainbow colours are named?
quiz.explain: It names red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet: 7 colours. 'Golden' describes the light, not a rainbow colour.
quiz.mistake: Misses a colour or counts 'golden' as a rainbow colour

quiz.q: Which pair of words rhymes?
quiz.explain: 'Rain' and 'train' end with the same '-ain' sound.
quiz.mistake: Picks words that go together in meaning instead of in sound

quiz.q: What is a group of lines in a poem called?
quiz.explain: Poems are made of stanzas. Stories are made of paragraphs.
quiz.mistake: Uses the word for stories instead of poems

quiz.q: Read: 'A shining bow of every hue.' Which word tells us the rainbow is bright?
quiz.explain: 'Shining' describes how bright the rainbow looks.
quiz.mistake: Picks the naming word instead of the describing word

teach.ask: Gappu looks at the sky: 'What are rhyming words? And what is a word picture in a poem?'
teach.praise: What a colourful explanation! My feathers are glowing like a rainbow!
teach.nudge: How do I know two words rhyme? And what does a word picture do?

learn.hook: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red. Say VIBGYOR fast three times!
points: A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through raindrops in the air.
Sunlight is made of seven colours. We remember their order as VIBGYOR.
To see a rainbow, stand with the sun behind you and the rain in front of you.
A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as': as green as a parrot; the rainbow is like a bridge.
Word pictures (imagery) help the reader see, hear, smell, taste or feel something.

example.q: Complete the simile: 'The mango leaves are as green as a ___.' Choose from: parrot, crow, cloud.
steps: A simile compares two things that share something.
We need something that is green.
A parrot is green; a crow is black and a rain cloud is grey.
example.answer: as green as a parrot

learn.reallife: After a monsoon shower in the evening, look at the sky away from the sun. You may spot a rainbow!

quiz.q: In VIBGYOR, what colour does the letter V stand for?
quiz.explain: VIBGYOR starts with violet. Note the spelling: v-i-o-l-e-t.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up violet with similar-sounding words

quiz.q: In VIBGYOR, which colour comes between green and orange?
quiz.explain: V-I-B-G-Y-O-R: after G (green) comes Y (yellow), then O (orange).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the order of the letters

quiz.q: When can we see a rainbow?
options: When there are no clouds or water
quiz.explain: A rainbow forms when sunlight passes through tiny drops of water in the air.
quiz.mistake: Does not know a rainbow needs both sunlight and water drops

quiz.q: Where should the sun be when you look at a rainbow?
quiz.explain: We see a rainbow when the sun is behind us and the raindrops are in front of us.
quiz.mistake: Thinks you must look towards the sun to see a rainbow

quiz.q: Which sentence is a simile?
options: Her smile was as bright as the sun.
quiz.explain: It compares her smile with the sun using 'as ... as'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence with a describing word is a simile

quiz.q: Complete the simile: 'as black as ___'
quiz.explain: Coal is black, so 'as black as coal' makes sense. Milk, snow and cotton are white.
quiz.mistake: Picks a thing that does not share the quality

quiz.q: On the outside edge of a rainbow, which colour do we usually see?
quiz.explain: In a rainbow, red is on the outer edge and violet is on the inner edge.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the bow starts with V because VIBGYOR does

quiz.q: Which sentence paints the best word picture?
options: Peacocks danced in the silver rain.
quiz.explain: 'Peacocks danced in the silver rain' helps us see colours and movement. That is imagery.
quiz.mistake: Picks a short, plain sentence that gives no picture

teach.ask: Gappu sings: 'What is VIBGYOR? And what is a simile?'
teach.praise: Seven colours and a simile! I feel as happy as a bird in the rain!
teach.nudge: Which colours are in VIBGYOR? And what words does a simile use?

learn.hook: The sky is bright. The rainbow is brighter. The sun is the brightest! Let's learn how describing words change.
points: Describing words (adjectives) tell us more about a noun: a colourful rainbow, five birds, a happy child.
To compare two things, we add -er or use 'more': brighter, more beautiful.
To compare more than two things, we add -est or use 'most': brightest, most beautiful.
Spelling changes: big-bigger-biggest, pretty-prettier-prettiest, wide-wider-widest.
Some words change completely: good-better-best, bad-worse-worst.

example.q: Choose: 'The rainbow is ___ than the grey clouds.' (bright, brighter, brightest)
steps: We are comparing two things: the rainbow and the clouds.
For two things we use the -er form.
The word 'than' also tells us to use the -er form.
example.answer: brighter

learn.reallife: In shops we hear, 'This one is cheaper,' and in sports, 'She is the fastest runner.' That is comparing!

quiz.q: Which word is an adjective in: 'A colourful rainbow appeared.'?
quiz.explain: 'Colourful' describes the rainbow, so it is an adjective.
quiz.mistake: Picks the noun or the verb

quiz.q: What is the comparative form of 'big'?
quiz.explain: Double the 'g' and add -er: bigger. 'Biggest' is the superlative.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the last letter

quiz.q: What is the superlative form of 'good'?
quiz.explain: Good changes completely: good, better, best.
quiz.mistake: Adds -est to an irregular adjective

quiz.q: Choose: 'Today is the ___ day of the year.' (hot)
quiz.explain: We compare one day with all the days of the year, so we use the superlative: hottest.
quiz.mistake: Uses the -er form when comparing more than two

quiz.q: Choose: 'The sky looks ___ than yesterday.' (clear)
quiz.explain: Two things are compared and the word 'than' is used, so we need 'clearer'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'more' and '-er' together

quiz.q: What is the superlative form of 'beautiful'?
quiz.explain: Long words use 'most' for the superlative: most beautiful.
quiz.mistake: Adds -est to a long word

quiz.q: What is the comparative form of 'pretty'?
quiz.explain: Change y to i and add -er: prettier.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the 'y' when adding -er

quiz.q: Which comparing sentence is correct?
options: An elephant is heavyer than a goat.
An elephant is more heavier than a goat.
An elephant is heavier than a goat.
An elephant is heaviest than a goat.
quiz.explain: 'Heavier' is the right comparative, and it goes with 'than'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up spelling rules or uses two comparatives together

teach.ask: Gappu puffs up: 'I am big, my mother is bigger. How do describing words change when we compare?'
teach.praise: Best explanation ever! That is the superlative, you know!
teach.nudge: Which ending do we use for two things? And which for more than two?

topics.title: A folk tale of a clever parrot

learn.hook: Can a little parrot be wiser than a whole court of ministers? In folk tales, anything can happen!
points: A folk tale is an old story that people told aloud for many years before it was written down.
Folk tales often begin with 'Long ago' or 'Once upon a time'.
They have kings, clever heroes and animals that can talk.
Most folk tales teach a lesson, called a moral.
India has many well-loved tales, such as the Panchatantra, the Jataka tales and stories of Tenali Rama.

example.q: Read: Long ago, a king had a parrot named Mithu who lived in a silver cage. One day, the king asked his court a riddle: 'What grows bigger the more you share it?' No minister could answer. Mithu called out, 'Happiness, Your Majesty!' The pleased king said, 'Ask for any reward.' Mithu replied, 'Please open my cage and let me fly.' The king kept his word. Now Mithu visits the palace garden every morning as a free friend. Why did Mithu ask for an open cage as his reward?
steps: The king offered any reward.
Mithu asked, 'Please open my cage and let me fly.'
He could have asked for anything, but he chose to fly free. Freedom mattered most to him.
example.answer: Because Mithu valued freedom more than any riches.

learn.reallife: Grandparents often tell folk tales at bedtime. Many of these stories are hundreds of years old and still teach us about kindness and cleverness.

games.title: Tale in order
games.prompt: Put the events of Mithu's tale in order
items: The king asks his court a riddle.
Mithu asks to be set free.
Mithu visits as a free friend.

games.title: Folk tale facts
items: Folk tales were told aloud for a long time before they were written down.
People passed them on by telling them to each other.
In many folk tales, animals can talk.
Talking animals, like Mithu, are common in folk tales.
The Panchatantra is a collection of Indian animal stories.
Its animal stories teach wise lessons.
In the tale, Mithu asked the king for a golden cage.
Mithu asked for the cage to be opened so he could fly.
In the tale, the minister answered the riddle first.
No minister could answer; Mithu did.

quiz.q: Read: 'A king had a parrot named Mithu who lived in a silver cage.' Where did Mithu live?
quiz.explain: The line says Mithu lived in a silver cage.
quiz.mistake: Remembers the wrong metal or place

quiz.q: Read: ''What grows bigger the more you share it?' ... Mithu called out, 'Happiness, Your Majesty!'' What was Mithu's answer to the riddle?
quiz.explain: Mithu said happiness grows bigger when you share it.
quiz.mistake: Does not find the answer in Mithu's words

quiz.q: Read: 'No minister could answer. Mithu called out, 'Happiness, Your Majesty!' The pleased king said, 'Ask for any reward.'' Why was the king pleased?
options: Mithu answered the riddle that nobody else could
quiz.explain: The ministers failed, but Mithu gave a clever answer.
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between the answer and the reward

quiz.q: Read: 'Mithu replied, 'Please open my cage and let me fly.'' What reward did Mithu ask for?
quiz.explain: Mithu asked for the cage to be opened so he could fly free.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a reward a parrot might like instead of reading the line

quiz.q: Read: 'The king kept his word.' What does 'kept his word' mean?
options: He did what he had promised
He wrote a word in a book
quiz.explain: To keep your word means to do what you promised. The king promised any reward.
quiz.mistake: Takes the phrase literally, word by word

quiz.q: What does the tale show about Mithu?
options: He was greedy and wanted gold
He was lazy and slept all day
He was clever and loved freedom
He was afraid of the king
quiz.explain: He solved the riddle (clever) and chose to be free (loved freedom).
quiz.mistake: Does not use the events to understand the character

quiz.q: Which lesson does Mithu's tale teach?
options: Freedom is more precious than a silver cage
quiz.explain: Mithu chose an open sky over a silver cage. That is the moral.
quiz.mistake: Picks a statement the story shows to be untrue

quiz.q: What is a folk tale?
options: A list of rules for a game
An old story passed on by people telling it
quiz.explain: Folk tales are old stories that were told aloud from one person to another, often for many years.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what a folk tale is

teach.ask: Gappu whistles: 'What is a folk tale? And what lesson did Mithu teach?'
teach.praise: Squawk! I would choose the open sky too! Great telling!
teach.nudge: What kind of story is a folk tale? And what was the lesson?

learn.hook: Clever, smart, wise... these words are cousins! Free and caged are opposites. Let's play with word meanings!
points: Synonyms are words with the same or nearly the same meaning: clever and smart; happy and glad.
Antonyms are words with opposite meanings: wise and foolish; open and shut.
Using synonyms makes our writing more interesting, so we do not repeat the same word.
Antonyms help us show contrast: The cage was shut, but now it is open.
Some words have more than one opposite: free can be the opposite of caged or of costly.

example.q: In 'The clever parrot asked the king to open the cage', give a synonym of 'clever' and an antonym of 'open'.
steps: Clever means quick at thinking. A word with a similar meaning is 'smart'.
The opposite of open is 'shut' or 'close'.
example.answer: Synonym of clever: smart. Antonym of open: shut.

learn.reallife: When you write a story, using synonyms like 'shouted, called, cried' instead of 'said' again and again makes it lively.

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'clever'?
quiz.explain: Clever and smart both mean quick at thinking and understanding.
quiz.mistake: Picks an antonym instead of a synonym

quiz.q: Which word is an antonym of 'wise'?
quiz.explain: Wise means having good sense; foolish means having poor sense.
quiz.mistake: Picks a synonym instead of an antonym

quiz.q: Mithu lived in a cage but now flies in the open sky. Which word is the opposite of 'caged'?
quiz.explain: A caged bird cannot fly away; a free bird can.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word with the same meaning as 'caged'

quiz.q: Which word means nearly the same as 'reward'?
quiz.explain: A reward is something given for doing well, like a prize.
quiz.mistake: Picks the opposite or an unrelated word from the story

quiz.q: Which word is an antonym of 'brave'?
quiz.explain: Brave means not afraid; cowardly means easily afraid.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up synonyms and antonyms

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'happy'?
quiz.explain: Happy and glad mean nearly the same thing.
quiz.mistake: Picks a feeling word that is not similar

quiz.q: Read: 'The parrot longed to fly over the hills.' What does 'longed' mean?
quiz.explain: To long for something is to wish for it very much.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'longed' is about length

quiz.q: Which pair of words are antonyms?
quiz.explain: Open and shut are opposites. The other pairs are synonyms.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any pair of related words are antonyms

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'What is the difference between a synonym and an antonym?'
teach.praise: Smart, clever, wise... you are all three!
teach.nudge: Which kind of word means the same? Which means the opposite?

topics.title: Joining ideas: and, but, because, so, or

learn.hook: Mithu was clever. Mithu won his freedom. Can we join these two sentences with one small word? Yes, we can!
points: Joining words (conjunctions) join words or sentences.
'and' adds one idea to another: The king and the queen smiled.
'but' shows a contrast: The cage was pretty, but Mithu wanted to be free.
'because' gives a reason; 'so' gives a result.
'or' gives a choice: Would you like a guava or a chilli?

example.q: Join with the best word: 'The parrot was clever. It won its freedom.'
steps: The first part is the reason; the second part is the result.
'so' joins a reason to its result.
Put a comma before 'so'.
example.answer: The parrot was clever, so it won its freedom.

learn.reallife: We use joining words all day: 'I am hungry, so I will eat.' 'Shall we play cricket or kho-kho?'

items.text: Mithu was happy ___ the cage was open.
It was raining, ___ we stayed inside.
I ran fast, ___ I missed the bus.

quiz.q: Choose: 'The riddle was hard, ___ nobody could answer it.'
quiz.explain: The hard riddle (reason) led to nobody answering (result), so we use 'so'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'but' or 'or' when the second part is a result of the first

quiz.q: Choose: 'The cage was beautiful, ___ Mithu wanted to be free.'
quiz.explain: The two ideas are in contrast: a beautiful cage, yet a wish for freedom. 'But' shows contrast.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'so' when the ideas do not follow from each other

quiz.q: Choose: 'Mithu was happy ___ he was free at last.'
quiz.explain: The second part gives the reason why Mithu was happy, so we use 'because'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up reason and result

quiz.q: Choose: 'Would you like a guava ___ a chilli, Mithu?'
quiz.explain: This is a choice between two things, so we use 'or'.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that a choice is being offered

quiz.q: Choose: 'The king ___ the queen laughed at the joke.'
quiz.explain: Both of them laughed. 'And' adds one person to the other.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that both did the action

quiz.q: Which word is the joining word in: 'I wanted to play, but it was raining.'?
quiz.explain: 'But' joins the two parts of the sentence.
quiz.mistake: Picks a verb instead of the joining word

quiz.q: Which joining word gives a reason?
quiz.explain: 'Because' tells us why something happened.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'because' (reason) with 'so' (result)

quiz.q: Which is the best way to join: 'Mithu flew away. He came back every morning.'?
options: Mithu flew away, because he came back every morning.
Mithu flew away, but he came back every morning.
Mithu flew away, or he came back every morning.
quiz.explain: Flying away and coming back are a contrast, so 'but' fits best.
quiz.mistake: Does not check if the joined sentence makes sense

teach.ask: Gappu has two twigs: 'How do I join two sentences? When do I use because and when do I use so?'
teach.praise: I joined my twigs and my sentences! Thank you, friend!
teach.nudge: Which word gives a reason? Which word shows a result?

learn.hook: Croak! Splash! Plop! Some words sound just like the noise they name. Let's hear them in a frog poem!
points: Animal poems tell us how an animal looks, moves and sounds.
Sound words copy the sound they name: croak, splash, plop, buzz, hiss.
Rhyming words at the ends of lines make a poem fun to read aloud: grows-toes, fall-all.
Poets choose action words that show movement: hop, leap, kick, dive.
Read the poem twice: once for fun, once to find the answers.

example.q: Read the poem: Down by the pond where the lotus grows, / Sits a little frog on his tippy toes. / 'Croak!' goes the frog when the raindrops fall, / 'Splash!' goes the frog, the happiest of all. / 'Plop!' in the water, kick, kick, kick, / His long back legs are strong and quick. Which sound words does the poet use?
steps: Look for words that copy a sound.
The frog says 'Croak!'
The water sounds are 'Splash!' and 'Plop!'
example.answer: Croak, splash and plop

learn.reallife: Comics use sound words all the time: BOOM! ZOOM! SPLASH! In the monsoon, you may hear real frogs croaking near ponds and fields.

games.title: About the frog poem
items: The frog sits by a pond where the lotus grows.
The first line says, 'Down by the pond where the lotus grows'.
The frog croaks when the raindrops fall.
'Croak!' goes the frog when the raindrops fall.
The poem says the frog has short, weak back legs.
It says his long back legs are strong and quick.
It copies the sound of something dropping into water.

quiz.q: Read: 'Down by the pond where the lotus grows, / Sits a little frog on his tippy toes.' Where does the frog sit?
options: By a pond where the lotus grows
quiz.explain: The first line tells us the frog is down by the pond where the lotus grows.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the first line of the poem

quiz.q: Read: ''Croak!' goes the frog when the raindrops fall.' What does the frog say when it rains?
quiz.explain: The line says 'Croak!' goes the frog. 'Splash' is the sound of the water.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the frog's call with the water sound

quiz.q: Read: ''Croak!' goes the frog when the raindrops fall, / 'Splash!' goes the frog, the happiest of all.' Which word rhymes with 'fall'?
quiz.explain: 'Fall' and 'all' end with the same sound.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that is in the lines but does not rhyme

quiz.q: Read: ''Plop!' in the water, kick, kick, kick, / His long back legs are strong and quick.' What helps the frog swim?
quiz.explain: The poem says his long back legs are strong and quick as he kicks in the water.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an adult frog swims with a tail like a tadpole

quiz.q: Which of these is a sound word?
quiz.explain: 'Splash' copies the sound of water. The others are not sound words.
quiz.mistake: Picks a naming or describing word

quiz.q: Read: ''Splash!' goes the frog, the happiest of all.' This happens when the raindrops fall. What does it show?
options: The frog is scared of rain
quiz.explain: Being 'the happiest of all' in the rain shows the frog loves wet weather.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the clue 'happiest'

quiz.q: Read: 'Sits a little frog on his tippy toes.' What does 'on his tippy toes' mean?
options: On the tips of his toes
quiz.explain: Tippy toes means standing up on the tips of your toes.
quiz.mistake: Guesses without picturing the words

quiz.q: Which sound word goes with a bee?
quiz.explain: Bees make a buzzing sound. Croak is for frogs, moo for cows, neigh for horses.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up animal sounds

teach.ask: Gappu hops like a frog: 'What are sound words? Which ones were in the frog poem?'
teach.praise: Croak, croak! That means 'well done' in frog language!
teach.nudge: What is a sound word? Can you tell me one from the poem?

learn.hook: A frog does not look like a frog when it is a baby! It starts life swimming like a tiny fish. Let's find out how!
points: A frog is an amphibian. It can live both in water and on land.
A frog's life cycle: eggs, then tadpole, then froglet, then adult frog.
Frogs lay their eggs in water. A tadpole lives in water and has a tail.
Most frogs catch insects with a long, sticky tongue.
To describe an animal, tell how it looks, how it moves, what it eats and where it lives.

example.q: Describe a frog in two sentences, using looks and movement.
steps: Looks: a frog has big round eyes, smooth damp skin and long back legs.
Movement: it hops on land and kicks to swim in water.
example.answer: A frog has big round eyes and smooth, damp skin. It hops on land and swims with its strong back legs.

learn.reallife: In the monsoon, ponds and puddles near fields fill with tadpoles. Look, but do not touch: frogs have delicate skin.

games.title: Frog life cycle
games.prompt: From the first stage to the last

quiz.q: A frog is an amphibian. What does this mean?
options: It can live both in water and on land
quiz.explain: Amphibians, like frogs, spend part of their life in water and part on land.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of 'amphibian'

quiz.q: What is the young frog that hatches from an egg called?
quiz.explain: A frog egg hatches into a tadpole. A froglet comes later, after the legs have grown.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up tadpole and froglet

quiz.q: In a frog's life cycle, what comes right after the eggs?
quiz.explain: Eggs hatch into tadpoles. Tadpoles later become froglets and then adult frogs.
quiz.mistake: Skips the tadpole stage

quiz.q: How do most frogs catch insects?
quiz.explain: A frog flicks out its long, sticky tongue to catch insects.
quiz.mistake: Thinks frogs hunt like cats or birds

quiz.q: Where do frogs lay their eggs?
quiz.explain: Frogs lay their eggs in water, such as ponds and puddles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all animals lay eggs on land

quiz.q: Which sentence tells how a frog moves?
options: The frog lives in a pond.
quiz.explain: 'Hops and leaps' are action words that show movement.
quiz.mistake: Picks a sentence about looks, food or home

quiz.q: Which words best describe the skin of most frogs?
quiz.explain: Most frogs have smooth, damp skin. Fur and feathers belong to other animals.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the body coverings of different animals

quiz.q: You are describing a frog. Which detail tells where it lives?
quiz.explain: 'It lives near ponds' tells us its home.
quiz.mistake: Picks a detail about looks, movement or sound

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'How does a tadpole become a frog? And how do I describe an animal?'
teach.praise: From egg to tadpole to frog! I want to watch a pond this monsoon!
teach.nudge: What comes after the eggs? And what can I tell about an animal when I describe it?

learn.hook: A baby frog is a tadpole. What is a baby cow called? And what do we call a group of bees? Let's find out!
points: Many animals have special names for their young ones: frog-tadpole, cat-kitten, dog-puppy.
More young ones: cow-calf, lion-cub, sheep-lamb, horse-foal, goat-kid, hen-chick, duck-duckling.
A collective noun names a group: a herd of cows, a flock of sheep, a swarm of bees.
More groups: a pride of lions, a school of fish, a troop of monkeys, a bunch of grapes.
We say 'a herd of elephants' because 'herd' names the whole group.

example.q: Fill in: 'A ___ of bees was buzzing near the hive.'
steps: We need a word for a group of bees.
Bees fly together in a swarm.
example.answer: swarm

learn.reallife: At a farm you may see a calf, a lamb and a kid. In a forest safari, you might spot a troop of monkeys or a herd of deer!

quiz.q: What is the young one of a lion called?
quiz.explain: A baby lion is a cub. Tiger and bear babies are also cubs.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up young-one names

quiz.q: What is the young one of a goat called?
quiz.explain: A baby goat is called a kid. A baby sheep is a lamb.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a goat with a sheep

quiz.q: What is the young one of a horse called?
quiz.explain: A baby horse is a foal.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the special name

quiz.q: What is the young one of a hen called?
quiz.explain: A hen's baby is a chick.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up young ones of birds and animals

quiz.q: Choose: 'A ___ of elephants walked to the river.'
quiz.explain: Large animals like elephants and cows move in a herd.
quiz.mistake: Uses the group word for birds or insects

quiz.q: Choose: 'A ___ of birds flew over the fields.'
quiz.explain: Birds fly together in a flock.
quiz.mistake: Uses the group word for cattle or lions

quiz.q: Which is a collective noun?
quiz.explain: 'Swarm' names a group of bees, so it is a collective noun.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the name of one animal is a collective noun

quiz.q: Choose: 'We saw a ___ of fish in the aquarium.'
quiz.explain: A group of fish swimming together is called a school.
quiz.mistake: Does not know this special group word

teach.ask: Gappu counts: 'One bee, two bees, a hundred bees! What do I call a group? And what is a baby lion?'
teach.praise: A flock of thank-yous from me and my bird friends!
teach.nudge: What is the word for a group? Can you name an animal baby too?

topics.title: The day the tank went dry

learn.hook: Imagine opening the tap to brush your teeth... and nothing comes out! Let's read about a street where that happened.
points: A story has a setting (where and when), characters (who) and a problem.
Look for clue words that tell when: 'one hot May morning', 'at noon', 'that evening'.
Look for the cause of the problem: why did something happen?
Sound words like 'drip, drip, drip' help us hear the story.
A good story often ends with a lesson the characters learn.

example.q: Read: One hot May morning, the taps in Gully No. 4 went dry. 'The tank on the roof is empty!' shouted Bunty. Everyone went up to the terrace to look. A pipe had been leaking all night, drip, drip, drip. A plumber fixed the pipe, and a water tanker came at noon. That evening, the children made a poster: 'Every drop counts! Close the tap!' Why did the taps go dry?
steps: Find the problem: the taps went dry and the tank was empty.
Find the cause: 'A pipe had been leaking all night'.
So the water slowly ran out through the leak.
example.answer: Because a pipe had been leaking all night and the tank became empty.

learn.reallife: In many Indian towns, water comes at fixed times and is stored in tanks. A small leak can waste a lot of it, so we must report leaks quickly.

games.title: True or false? (from the story)
items: The story happens on a hot May morning.
The tank was on the roof.
Bunty shouted, 'The tank on the roof is empty!'
The water tanker came at midnight.
The children made a poster about saving water.
It said, 'Every drop counts! Close the tap!'

games.title: Story order
games.prompt: Put the story events in order
items: Bunty finds the tank is empty.

quiz.q: Read: 'One hot May morning, the taps in Gully No. 4 went dry.' When did the taps go dry?
quiz.explain: The line says 'One hot May morning'.
quiz.mistake: Does not find the time words in the line

quiz.q: Read: 'A pipe had been leaking all night, drip, drip, drip.' Why was the tank empty?
options: A pipe had been leaking all night
quiz.explain: The leak let the water drip out all night until the tank was empty.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a reason instead of finding it in the story

quiz.q: Read: 'A plumber fixed the pipe, and a water tanker came at noon.' Who fixed the pipe?
quiz.explain: The line clearly says a plumber fixed the pipe.
quiz.mistake: Picks a character without checking the line

quiz.q: Read: 'A plumber fixed the pipe, and a water tanker came at noon.' When did the water tanker come?
quiz.explain: Noon means twelve o'clock in the daytime.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of 'noon'

quiz.q: Read: 'A pipe had been leaking all night, drip, drip, drip.' What do the words 'drip, drip, drip' tell us?
options: Water was falling drop by drop
quiz.explain: 'Drip' is the sound of single drops falling, again and again.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a leak must be a big gush

quiz.q: Read: 'The children made a poster: 'Every drop counts! Close the tap!'' What was the poster about?
quiz.explain: 'Every drop counts' and 'Close the tap' are about saving water.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the poster's words

quiz.q: What does 'Every drop counts' mean?
options: Even a little water is important
quiz.explain: It means even small amounts of water matter, so we should not waste any.
quiz.mistake: Takes the words 'counts' literally

quiz.q: Read: ''The tank on the roof is empty!' shouted Bunty.' Where was the water tank?
quiz.explain: Bunty says 'The tank on the roof'.
quiz.mistake: Does not find the place word in the line

teach.ask: Gappu drinks from a puddle: 'Why did the tank go dry? What did the children learn?'
teach.praise: Drip, drip, hooray! You explained it so well!
teach.nudge: What caused the tank to go empty? And what lesson did the children share?

learn.hook: 'Close the tap!' 'Fix the leak!' Instructions are short and bossy... but they help save water!
points: An instruction tells someone what to do. It often begins with an action word: Close, Turn, Use, Fix.
To say what not to do, begin with 'Do not' or 'Don't': Don't leave the tap running.
Add 'Please' to make an instruction polite: Please turn off the tap.
Ways to save water: turn off the tap while brushing, use a bucket to bathe, fix leaks, reuse water for plants.
Rainwater harvesting means collecting rainwater and storing it to use later.

example.q: Change into an instruction: 'You should turn off the tap while brushing your teeth.'
steps: An instruction starts with the action word.
Remove 'You should'.
Begin with 'Turn'.
example.answer: Turn off the tap while brushing your teeth.

learn.reallife: School posters, recipe steps and game rules are full of instructions. Writing your own 'Save Water' rules for home is a great project!

games.title: Save or waste?
items: Turning off the tap while brushing
Watering plants with water used to wash vegetables
Washing a scooter with a running pipe

quiz.explain: It tells someone what to do and begins with an action word.

quiz.q: Which instruction tells what NOT to do?

quiz.explain: We collect rainwater from roofs and store it in tanks or let it soak into the ground.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'harvesting' must be about crops

quiz.explain: Reusing clean leftover water for plants saves fresh water.
quiz.mistake: Does not think of reusing water

quiz.explain: 'Please' makes an instruction polite.

topics.title: Compound words: two words become one

learn.hook: Rain + water = rainwater. Sun + flower = sunflower. Two small words can join to make a brand-new word!
points: A compound word is made by joining two words: rain + coat = raincoat.
The two parts often give a clue to the meaning: a toothbrush is a brush for teeth.
Some compound words have a new meaning: a butterfly is not made of butter!
Water words: rainwater, waterfall, watermelon.
Home words: bathroom, rooftop, teapot, bedroom.

example.q: Which two words make 'rainwater', and what does it mean?
steps: Split the word: rain + water.
Put the meanings together: water that comes from the rain.
example.answer: rain + water: water from the rain

learn.reallife: Look around your home: bedroom, toothpaste, cupboard, doorbell. Compound words are everywhere!

quiz.q: Which is a compound word?
quiz.explain: Toothbrush is made of two words: tooth + brush.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a word with an ending like -ing is a compound word

quiz.q: sun + light = ?
quiz.explain: Joining sun and light gives sunlight.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word with only one of the parts

quiz.q: Which two words make 'bathroom'?
quiz.explain: 'Bathroom' is a room for taking a bath: bath + room.

quiz.q: Which word can join 'foot' to make a compound word?
quiz.explain: Foot + ball = football.

quiz.q: What is a 'waterfall'?
options: A glass of water that fell
quiz.explain: A waterfall is water flowing down from a high place, like a cliff.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a compound word?

quiz.q: roof + top = ?
quiz.explain: Joining roof and top gives rooftop, the top of a roof.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that only sounds similar

quiz.explain: Tea + pot = teapot.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word with only one part of the meaning

teach.ask: Gappu tries: 'Bird + house = birdhouse? What is a compound word?'
teach.praise: Yes! Birdhouse is a compound word, and now I am super-happy!
teach.nudge: How is a compound word made? Can you give me an example?

topics.title: Gilli danda: a game from long ago

learn.hook: No batteries, no screen, just two wooden sticks and a lot of fun! Let's read about gilli danda.
points: Traditional games have been played in India for a very long time.
Gilli danda is played with two pieces of wood: a small gilli with pointed ends and a longer stick called the danda.
Other traditional games are kho-kho, kabaddi, pitthu (lagori) and langdi.
These games need very little equipment and can be played in any open space.
Playing together teaches us teamwork, taking turns and fair play.

example.q: Read: After school, Irfan and Gopal raced to the open ground with their gilli and danda. The gilli was a small piece of wood with pointed ends. The danda was a longer stick. Gopal tapped one end of the gilli and it flew up. Whack! He hit it far across the ground. Irfan ran and caught it. 'Out!' he laughed. They took turns and played till sunset. Then they walked home together, still laughing. What do you need to play gilli danda?
steps: Find the things named: the gilli and the danda.
The gilli is a small piece of wood with pointed ends.
The danda is a longer stick.
example.answer: A small gilli with pointed ends and a longer stick called the danda.

learn.reallife: Ask your grandparents which games they played as children. Many will smile and say 'gilli danda' or 'kho-kho'!

games.title: True or false? (from the story)
items: Irfan and Gopal played after school.
The gilli is longer than the danda.
The gilli is small; the danda is the longer stick.
They took turns and played till sunset.
They walked home together, still laughing.

games.title: Game and what it needs
pairs: a pile of flat stones and a ball
a board, coins and a striker

quiz.q: Read: 'The gilli was a small piece of wood with pointed ends.' What does the gilli look like?
options: A small piece of wood with pointed ends
quiz.explain: The line describes the gilli as small, wooden and pointed at the ends.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the gilli with things used in other games

quiz.q: Read: 'The danda was a longer stick.' What is the danda?
quiz.explain: The danda is the longer stick used to hit the gilli.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the danda with the gilli

quiz.q: Read: 'Gopal tapped one end of the gilli and it flew up. Whack! He hit it far across the ground.' What did Gopal do first?
options: He hit it far across the ground
He tapped one end of the gilli
quiz.explain: First he tapped the gilli to make it fly up. Then he hit it.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of actions

quiz.q: Read: 'Irfan ran and caught it. 'Out!' he laughed.' Who said 'Out!'?
quiz.explain: Irfan caught the gilli and laughed, 'Out!'
quiz.mistake: Does not see who 'he' refers to

quiz.q: Read: 'Whack! He hit it far across the ground.' What kind of word is 'Whack'?
quiz.explain: 'Whack' copies the sound of a stick hitting something.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise a sound word

quiz.q: Read: 'They took turns and played till sunset. Then they walked home together, still laughing.' What do these lines show about the boys?
options: They were good friends who played fairly
They did not like each other
They were tired of the game
quiz.explain: Taking turns and laughing together shows friendship and fair play.
quiz.mistake: Does not use clues to understand characters

quiz.q: Which of these is a traditional Indian game?
quiz.explain: Kho-kho has been played in Indian villages and schools for a long time.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a new screen game is traditional

quiz.q: Why can gilli danda be played almost anywhere there is open space?
options: It needs only two wooden sticks
quiz.explain: Gilli danda needs very little: a gilli and a danda.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect simple equipment with easy play

teach.ask: Gappu holds two twigs: 'Is this gilli danda? Tell me about this game and other old Indian games!'
teach.praise: Whack! I want to play gilli danda with my bird friends now!
teach.nudge: What are the gilli and the danda? Can you name another traditional game?

topics.title: Action words and how we do them

learn.hook: Run! Hit! Catch! Games are full of action words. And HOW do we do them? Quickly, happily, carefully!
points: Verbs are action words: run, hit, catch, throw, jump.
Adverbs tell us more about a verb: how, when or where it happens.
Many adverbs end in -ly: quick-quickly, soft-softly, careful-carefully.
If the word ends in y, change y to i and add -ly: happy-happily, easy-easily.
Some adverbs do not end in -ly: fast, well, hard, soon, here.

example.q: Find the verb and the adverb: 'Gopal hit the gilli hard.'
steps: The action is 'hit', so 'hit' is the verb.
'Hard' tells us how he hit it, so 'hard' is the adverb.
example.answer: Verb: hit. Adverb: hard.

learn.reallife: Sports commentators use adverbs all the time: 'She ran swiftly! He bowled cleverly!'

quiz.q: Which word is the verb in: 'Irfan caught the gilli.'?
quiz.explain: 'Caught' is the action.
quiz.mistake: Picks the naming word

quiz.q: Which word is the adverb in: 'Gopal ran quickly to the ground.'?
quiz.explain: 'Quickly' tells us how Gopal ran.
quiz.mistake: Picks the verb instead of the word that describes it

quiz.q: Change 'happy' into an adverb.
quiz.explain: Change y to i and add -ly: happily.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the 'y' before adding -ly

quiz.q: Choose: 'The children played ___ in the park.'
quiz.explain: We need a word that tells how they played, so we use the adverb 'happily'.
quiz.mistake: Uses an adjective where an adverb is needed

quiz.q: Which is an action word?
quiz.explain: 'Throw' is something you do. The others are describing or naming words.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up verbs with nouns and adjectives

quiz.q: Read: 'Meena plays kabaddi well.' What does 'well' tell us?
quiz.explain: 'Well' is an adverb that tells how she plays.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that an adverb can describe how

quiz.q: Change 'careful' into an adverb.
quiz.explain: Just add -ly: careful + ly = carefully, with two l's.
quiz.mistake: Drops one 'l' when adding -ly

quiz.q: Choose: 'The friends cheered ___ when Gopal hit the gilli far.'
quiz.explain: We need an adverb to tell how they cheered: loudly.
quiz.mistake: Uses a naming or describing word after the verb

teach.ask: Gappu flaps fast: 'I am flying quickly! Which word is the action and which tells how?'
teach.praise: I flapped happily and learnt quickly! Thank you!
teach.nudge: Which word is the action? And which word tells how the action is done?

learn.hook: Where did the gilli go? Over the wall? Under the bench? Behind the tree? Words of place help us find it!
points: Good friends take turns, share and play fair, whether they win or lose.
Prepositions are words that tell where something is: in, on, under, over, behind, near.
'between' is used for something in the middle of two: The ball is between Irfan and Gopal.
'across' means from one side to the other: He hit the gilli across the ground.
Words in a sentence must be in the right order to make sense.

example.q: Fill in: 'The gilli flew ___ the wall and landed in the garden next door.'
steps: The gilli went up and to the other side of the wall.
A word for going above something to the other side is 'over'.
example.answer: over

learn.reallife: When you tell a friend 'Your bat is behind the door' or 'My bottle is in my bag', you use prepositions.

items.text: The ball rolled ___ the bed, so we had to crawl to get it.

games.title: Make a sentence
games.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence

quiz.q: Choose: 'We ran ___ the ground to reach the other side.'
quiz.explain: 'Across' means from one side to the other.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of 'across'

quiz.q: Choose: 'Rani is sitting ___ Meena and Joseph.'
quiz.explain: We use 'between' for someone in the middle of two people.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'among' for only two people

quiz.q: Which word is a preposition in: 'The danda is near the door.'?
quiz.explain: 'Near' tells us where the danda is.

quiz.explain: If Gopal is behind the tree, the tree blocks Irfan's view.

quiz.q: Choose: 'Put your shoes ___ the shelf.'
quiz.explain: Things rest on a shelf.

quiz.q: Which shows fair play in a game?

quiz.mistake: Thinks winning matters more than fairness

quiz.q: Your friend loses the game and looks sad. What is the kind thing to say?
options: Well played! Let's play again tomorrow.
quiz.explain: Good friends cheer each other up, whether they win or lose.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about the friend's feelings

quiz.q: Which sentence has the words in the right order?
quiz.explain: An English sentence usually goes: who (Gopal), action (hit), what (the gilli), then more (far).
quiz.mistake: Does not follow the who-action-what order

teach.ask: Gappu is lost: 'Where is my nest? Behind the tree? What are words of place called? And how do good friends play?'
teach.praise: Found it! My nest is on the branch, behind the leaves. Thank you, friend!
teach.nudge: Which words tell us where something is? And what do good friends do when they play?

topics.title: A fair decision in the village

learn.hook: Two farmers, one calf, and a big quarrel! How can the village find out the truth fairly? Let's read!
points: A panchayat is a group of people who look after the matters of a village.
A fair decision is made after listening to everyone, without taking sides.
A good judge stays calm, asks questions and looks for the truth.
In stories, a clever test can help find out the truth.
Fairness means treating everyone the same way, whether they are rich or poor, friend or stranger.

example.q: Read: In the village of Rampur, two farmers, Harish and Anil, both said a lost calf was theirs. They went to the panchayat. The Sarpanch listened to both of them calmly. Then she said, 'Let the calf choose.' The calf was set free in the village square. It ran straight to Anil's cow and began to drink milk. 'The calf belongs to Anil,' said the Sarpanch. Harish said sorry, and the two farmers shook hands. Why was letting the calf choose a fair test?
steps: A young calf goes to its own mother to drink milk.
Neither farmer could control what the calf did.
So the calf's choice showed the truth, without taking sides.
example.answer: Because the calf would run to its own mother, and nobody could cheat.

learn.reallife: In class, when two friends both want the same seat, a fair teacher listens to both before deciding. That is what a good panchayat does too.

games.title: Story order
games.prompt: Put the story events in order
items: Two farmers both claim the calf.
The calf runs to Anil's cow.

games.title: True or false? (from the story)
items: The Sarpanch listened to only one farmer.
She listened to both of them calmly.
The Sarpanch said, 'Let the calf choose.'
The calf ran to Harish's cow.
It ran straight to Anil's cow.
Harish said sorry at the end.
Harish said sorry, and they shook hands.

quiz.q: Read: 'Harish and Anil both said a lost calf was theirs. They went to the panchayat.' Why did the farmers go to the panchayat?
options: They wanted to buy a cow
They wanted to build a road
Both said the calf was theirs
quiz.explain: Both farmers claimed the same calf, so they needed a fair decision.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a reason not given in the lines

quiz.explain: She listened to both, and she stayed calm. That is fair.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the word 'both'

quiz.q: Read: 'Then she said, 'Let the calf choose.'' What was the Sarpanch's idea?
options: To give the calf to herself
quiz.explain: Her plan was to let the calf show whose it was.
quiz.mistake: Picks an unfair idea that is not in the story

quiz.q: Read: 'It ran straight to Anil's cow and began to drink milk.' What did the calf do?
options: It ran to Anil's cow and drank milk
It ran out of the village
quiz.explain: The calf went straight to its mother, Anil's cow.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two farmers

options: Peacefully, with the farmers shaking hands
quiz.explain: Saying sorry and shaking hands shows the quarrel ended in peace.
quiz.mistake: Expects a quarrel to end badly

quiz.q: Read: 'The Sarpanch listened to both of them calmly.' What does 'calmly' mean?
quiz.explain: Calm means peaceful and not upset. 'Calmly' is how she listened.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'calmly' with words for strong feelings

quiz.q: What makes a decision fair?
options: Listening to everyone and not taking sides
quiz.explain: A fair judge hears all sides and looks for the truth.
quiz.mistake: Thinks being fair means helping someone you like

quiz.q: Read: 'The calf belongs to Anil,' said the Sarpanch. Who is the Sarpanch?
options: The head of the village panchayat
quiz.explain: The Sarpanch is the head of the gram panchayat.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the word 'Sarpanch'

teach.ask: Gappu and his brother both want the same worm! 'How can we decide fairly, like the panchayat?'
teach.praise: We shared the worm fairly! You would make a great Sarpanch!
teach.nudge: What should a fair judge do before deciding? Should we listen to one side or both?

topics.title: Words of fairness and their opposites

learn.hook: Fair or unfair? Honest or dishonest? Just add a little word-part in front, and the meaning flips!
points: A gram panchayat looks after a village: roads, clean water, drains and more.
The head of a gram panchayat is called the Sarpanch. The members are chosen by the villagers by voting.
Words about fairness: fair, honest, truth, justice, decision, witness.
A prefix is a word-part added to the beginning of a word. un-, dis- and in- can make opposites.
fair-unfair, kind-unkind, honest-dishonest, agree-disagree, justice-injustice, correct-incorrect.

example.q: Make the opposite with a prefix: 'It was a fair decision.'
steps: The word to change is 'fair'.
The prefix 'un-' makes the opposite of 'fair'.
un + fair = unfair.
example.answer: It was an unfair decision.

learn.reallife: When we play, we often say 'That's unfair!' Now you know that 'un-' is the part that flips 'fair' into its opposite.

quiz.q: What is the head of a gram panchayat called?
quiz.explain: The Sarpanch leads the gram panchayat.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the heads of different groups

quiz.q: How are the members of a gram panchayat chosen?
options: They are picked by lucky draw
quiz.explain: Panchayat members are elected: the villagers vote to choose them.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that panchayat members are elected

quiz.q: Which is the opposite of 'fair'?
quiz.explain: We add 'un-' to fair to make 'unfair'.
quiz.mistake: Picks the wrong prefix

quiz.q: Which is the opposite of 'honest'?
quiz.explain: We add 'dis-' to honest to make 'dishonest'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'un-' for every opposite

quiz.q: Which is the opposite of 'justice'?
quiz.explain: We add 'in-' to justice to make 'injustice'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'un-' or 'dis-' for every opposite

quiz.q: Read: 'The panchayat gave its decision.' What is a 'decision'?
quiz.explain: A decision is what you choose after thinking about something.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the word 'decision'

quiz.q: Which prefix makes the opposite of 'agree'?
quiz.explain: dis + agree = disagree.
quiz.mistake: Picks a prefix that does not make a real word

quiz.q: Read: 'The two farmers had a quarrel.' What is a 'quarrel'?
quiz.explain: A quarrel is when people argue angrily.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a meaning that does not fit the sentence

teach.ask: Gappu frowns: 'My brother took my worm. That's ... disfair? Unfair? How do we make opposites with prefixes?'
teach.praise: That's FAIR! Now I know the prefixes!
teach.nudge: What is a prefix? Which one makes the opposite of 'fair'?

learn.hook: "Let the calf choose," said the Sarpanch. See those little marks? They hold the exact words someone said!
points: Speech marks (inverted commas) go around the exact words a person says.
The spoken words begin with a capital letter: The Sarpanch said, "Let the calf choose."
A comma usually comes after 'said' or 'asked' when it comes before the spoken words.
The full stop, question mark or exclamation mark goes inside the closing speech marks.
Use 'asked' for a question, 'replied' for an answer and 'shouted' for loud words.

example.q: Punctuate: the sarpanch said let the calf choose
steps: Begin the sentence with a capital: The Sarpanch.
Put a comma after 'said'.
Put speech marks around her words and begin them with a capital L.
Put the full stop inside the closing speech marks.
example.answer: The Sarpanch said, "Let the calf choose."

learn.reallife: Comics show speech in bubbles. In stories and newspapers, speech marks do the same job.

items.text: "It is in the field," ___ his son, answering Anil.

games.title: Speech mark rules
items: Speech marks go around the exact words a person says.
They show the words just as they were spoken.

We use 'asked' when someone answers a question.
We use 'replied' or 'answered' for an answer.
In 'Ravi said, "I am ready."', the full stop is inside the speech marks.
The full stop comes before the closing speech marks.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses speech marks correctly?
options: The Sarpanch said, "Let the calf choose."

"The Sarpanch said, let the calf choose."

quiz.explain: Only her exact words are inside the speech marks, and they start with a capital.

quiz.q: Read: Harish asked, "Is the calf mine?" What were Harish's exact words?
options: Harish asked is the calf mine
quiz.explain: The words inside the speech marks are exactly what he said.

quiz.q: Choose: "Where is my calf?" ___ Anil.
quiz.explain: Anil is asking a question, so 'asked' fits best.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the question mark

quiz.q: What do speech marks show?
quiz.explain: Speech marks hold the words a person actually spoke.
quiz.mistake: Confuses speech marks with other punctuation

quiz.q: In 'The Sarpanch said, "let the calf choose."', what is wrong?
options: 'let' should begin with a capital L
quiz.explain: The first spoken word always begins with a capital letter.
quiz.mistake: Does not know spoken words begin with a capital

quiz.q: Which word fits: "The calf is mine," ___ Anil, after the Sarpanch asked him.
quiz.explain: He is answering the Sarpanch, so 'replied' fits.
quiz.mistake: Uses a question word for an answer

quiz.q: Where does the question mark go in: Anil asked, "Is this your calf"
quiz.explain: It goes inside: Anil asked, "Is this your calf?"
quiz.mistake: Puts the end mark outside the speech marks

quiz.q: Choose the right punctuation: Anil said ___ "Thank you."
quiz.explain: A comma comes after 'said' and before the speech marks.
quiz.mistake: Uses an end mark in the middle of a sentence

teach.ask: Gappu chirps something: 'How do I write down exactly what I said in a story?'
teach.praise: "Thank you!" said Gappu. See? I used speech marks!
teach.nudge: Which marks go around spoken words? And how does the first spoken word begin?

topics.title: A poem about the work people do

learn.hook: The baker, the painter, the farmer, the postman... Every day we see people doing different work. Which would you like to do?
points: Poems about work show us the many jobs people do around us.
A vocation is the work a person chooses or feels they are meant to do.
Children often dream about what they will be when they grow up.
Each pair of lines in this poem rhymes: bread-shed, wheat-street, tall-all.
Every kind of honest work is useful and deserves respect.

example.q: Read the poem: I watch the baker knead the bread, / I watch the painter paint the shed. / The farmer sows the seeds of wheat, / The postman cycles down our street. / I wonder, when I'm grown and tall, / Which one I'll be, or maybe all! What does the child in the poem wonder about?
steps: Look at the last two lines.
'I wonder, when I'm grown and tall, / Which one I'll be, or maybe all!'
So the child wonders which work they will do when they grow up.
example.answer: Which of these jobs they will do when they grow up, or maybe all of them!

learn.reallife: Think of the people who help your family every day: the vegetable seller, the bus driver, the doctor, the teacher. Each has a vocation.

games.title: About the poem
items: In the poem, the painter paints the shed.
'I watch the painter paint the shed.'
The farmer sows seeds of rice.
The poem says the farmer sows the seeds of wheat.
The postman cycles down the street.
The child has already chosen one job.
The child still wonders 'Which one I'll be, or maybe all!'

quiz.q: Read: 'I watch the baker knead the bread.' What is the baker doing?
quiz.explain: The line says the baker kneads the bread.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the workers in the poem

quiz.q: Read: 'The postman cycles down our street.' Who cycles down the street?
quiz.explain: The line names the postman.
quiz.mistake: Picks a worker from another line

quiz.q: Read: 'The farmer sows the seeds of wheat.' What does the farmer sow?
quiz.explain: The farmer sows wheat seeds.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the line carefully

quiz.q: Read: 'The farmer sows the seeds of wheat, / The postman cycles down our street.' Which word rhymes with 'wheat'?
quiz.explain: 'Wheat' and 'street' end with the same sound.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word from the lines that does not rhyme

quiz.q: Read: 'I wonder, when I'm grown and tall, / Which one I'll be, or maybe all!' What is the child wondering?
options: Which work they will do when they grow up
quiz.explain: The child wonders which of these jobs they will choose one day.
quiz.mistake: Takes the words 'grown and tall' too literally

quiz.q: Read: 'I watch the baker knead the bread.' What does 'knead' mean?
options: To press and fold dough with the hands
quiz.explain: Knead means to press and fold dough. It sounds like 'need', but the meaning is different.

learn.hook: A person who teaches is a teacher. A person who sails is a sailor. Can you guess what a person who paints is called?
points: An occupation is the work a person does to earn a living.
Many worker words are made by adding -er: teach-teacher, farm-farmer, bake-baker.
Some add -or: act-actor, sail-sailor, direct-director.
Some end in -ist or -ian: art-artist, violin-violinist, music-musician, science-scientist.
Some worker words are special: a cobbler mends shoes, a carpenter works with wood.

example.q: What do we call a person who paints, and how is the word made?
steps: Start with the action word: paint.
Add the ending -er.
paint + er = painter.
example.answer: painter

learn.reallife: On Career Day at school, children dress up as doctors, pilots, scientists and chefs. Each worker word tells what the person does!

quiz.explain: Science becomes scientist.
